The history of the Internet demonstrates that the first practical form of any kind of online 'thing' tends to become the definitive one, and remains so unless something radically disrupts it. Amazon, Facebook, Twitter, eBay, Uber, you name it, all have their competition that never surpass them even if 'better' in some ways. The first brand to make an idea work online tends to become the definition of the activity.

In business in general, follow-on competition tends to pay more/work harder for market share. When access is free, there isn't much incentive to go somewhere else. Indeed, there's a disincentive in that every other follow-on has its own learning curve for the new user. It's very hard for a follow-on venture to knock off the established form/brand unless it can be very disruptive in some way, offering new capability, productivity, etc. One example is Google. Yahoo was the first form of what Google now dominates as. It was surpassed by Google because Google invested in a critical technology Yahoo ignored for too long; automated search engines. When Yahoo started web 'indexes' were made manually and you searched them like an encyclopedia. You literally had people sitting in offices scanning or 'crawling' known web pages for links to other new web pages and adding them to subject/keyword indexes. Then they started making 'web crawler' programs that would automatically scan pages for links and embedded keywords to help index them--which at first was easily spoofed by marketing con-artists. When Google came along they recognized the value of more active, sophisticated, web searching with the ability to understand page content and the ability to parse complex search phrases. They developed a much more advanced, faster, web crawling and page ranking algorithm--which is what started them on the path to AI research. Google recognized that searching was the first thing most people (then) did when they went online and how this could integrate into ad revenue based on promoting pages higher in search results. Yahoo was too late in recognizing this, focussing instead on being the Internet's 'home page', and was out-disrupted. The brand 'Google' soon became the word defining web search online. No one ever said; "Let's yahoo that name online..." Now it's almost impossible for anyone to challenge Google's place, even though there are many other search engines, including one sponsored by the Microsoft behemoth. A new technology--perhaps the Semantic Web--may be needed to disrupt Google.

Reddit is a somewhat similar story to Google with a twist. Originally, Digg was the dominant social news aggregator site (which have their roots in Usenet) and it functioned much like Reddit. Reddit didn't disrupt Digg so much as Digg management going insane and destroying their own creation through incompetence. They disrupted themselves with a succession of radical platform redesigns that slowly stripped the 'social' out of the social news aggregator while Reddit, recognizing the importance of that, sought the cultivation of a positive user 'culture', helping them to fill the vacuum Digg's management made themselves. (ask yourself, what sort of user culture does Voat have? Is it a positive culture that equates, in advertisers' minds, to a valuable user demographic?)

Whatever you think of Reddit's management, it's now the definitive social news aggregator. No one else is really improving the nature/quality of that activity. It's really hard to knock them off the top of the hill unless they follow in Digg's footsteps (which certainly could happen) or you bring something really new to the table --and the 'freedom' to post s*** like this doesn't amount to much. So far Reddit's management missteps haven't yet been enough to seriously hurt its image, user culture, and most importantly it apparent user demographic. No one's yet counting or talking much about the flow of Reddit refugees like they once did with Digg.
